title: Be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:1–9)
hookLine: Moses is gone, and Joshua is told three times: be strong, don't be afraid

cards: "Moses my servant is dead." That is how God's first words to Joshua in this book begin. No easing in.
Moses stood before Pharaoh, went up the mountain, spoke with God for everyone. Joshua was his assistant; the opening verse calls him "Moses' minister."

Now the people are camped by the Jordan River, the land is on the far side, and the one who always seemed to know what came next is gone. The same sentence moves on: "now therefore arise, go over this Jordan."
And before Joshua takes a single step, God tells him the same thing again, and again.

teach.b: Year three is the long story: Israel after the wilderness, from Joshua to the return from exile. It opens with a handover. In nine verses, God tells Joshua three times to be strong.
In the King James Bible, verse six: "Be strong and of a good courage." Verse seven pushes further: "Only be thou strong and very courageous."
Verse nine makes it a question: "Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest."
Some readers notice that people rarely need telling three times unless something in them is shaking. The text never says what Joshua felt. It only gives him the words.
Now look where the courage comes from.

teach.h: THE REASON POINTS AWAY FROM HIM.
teach.b: Each reason points away from Joshua.
Verse five: "as I was with Moses, so I will be with thee: I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee." The strength rests on company, not on confidence. And there's a surprise tucked in the middle.
Verse eight ties the command to a book: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night."
The first thing asked of a new leader about to cross a river is to keep reading. Some Christians turn to this chapter at new starts.

teach.h: I WILL NOT FAIL THEE, NOR FORSAKE THEE.
teach.b: The line to carry is the quiet one in verse five: I will not fail thee.

how: Some Christians turn to Joshua 1:9 before a hard new beginning, such as a move, a new job or an exam, and some memorize it or keep it written where they will see it.

games.q: you're Joshua. Moses, the leader you served, is dead, and the river is in front of you. what does God say next?
o: take time to grieve before anything else.
wait for a new Moses to be sent.
games.why: "Moses my servant is dead; now therefore arise, go over this Jordan." the loss and the call arrive in the same sentence.

practice: Let one small, real thing come to mind that you've been putting off because it unsettles you a little: a phone call, an apology, a first page.

Don't solve it; just name it, and sit with the words Joshua heard: be strong, be not afraid. If you pray, hold that one thing up and rest on the promise, I will not fail thee; if you don't, simply breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Chazak. Hebrew for be strong: what God tells Joshua three times as Moses' work passes into his hands, courage resting on company, not on confidence.

orig.note: Hebrew: be strong and be bold, the pair God speaks to Joshua in verses 6, 7 and 9.
